title: Give bare `dict`, `set` and `frozenset` return annotations structured output
prompt:
Make the change described below to the repository in the current directory.
Work until the change is complete. Do not open a pull request, push, or fetch anything from the network.

# Give bare `dict`, `set` and `frozenset` return annotations structured output

Fixes #3725

A bare `-> dict` now gets the same structured output as `-> dict[str, Any]`, and a bare `-> set` / `-> frozenset` is wrapped in `{"result": ...}` like their parameterized forms. A bare `-> list` / `-> tuple` deliberately stays unstructured, and `structured_output=True` now wraps it instead of raising.

## Motivation and Context

Bare builtins fell through to the "other class" branch of `_create_output_model`, where `get_type_hints(dict)` is `{}`, so the tool silently got no `outputSchema` and no `structuredContent`. With `structured_output=True` it raised `return type <class 'dict'> is not serializable`, which reads as if a dict weren't serializable.

| Annotation | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| `-> dict` | no schema | `{"type": "object", "additionalProperties": true}`, unwrapped |
| `-> set`, `-> frozenset` | no schema | wrapped, `{"type": "array", "uniqueItems": true, "items": {}}` |
| `-> list`, `-> tuple` | no schema | no schema (on purpose); wrapped with `structured_output=True` |

### Why bare `list` / `tuple` stay unstructured

`_convert_to_content` renders content blocks found in a list or tuple as blocks, and `_returns_content` already opts `list[ImageContent]` and friends out of structured output so the image isn't also echoed into `structuredContent`. A bare `list` says nothing about its items, so it may hold blocks too: a `-> list` tool returning `[Image(...), {...}]` would send the image twice, once as a block and once as base64 in `structuredContent`. Some clients then render the JSON instead of the picture, others put the base64 in the model's context. `set` / `frozenset` can't hold content blocks (they aren't hashable), so wrapping them is safe.

FastMCP made the same call (`function_parsing.py`: bare `list`/`tuple` produce no output schema for this reason, while bare `dict` and `set` get one). `list[X]` and `structured_output=True` remain the explicit opt-ins.

## Breaking Changes

Tools annotated with a bare `dict`, `set` or `frozenset` start publishing an `outputSchema` and validating their result against it, exactly as `dict[str, Any]` / `set[Any]` do today. Values that used to be dumped as text with `to_json(..., fallback=str)` and now fail as a tool error (`is_error=True`):

- a bare-`dict` tool returning non-`str` keys, e.g. `{1: "a"}`;
- a `None` return from a `-> dict` / `-> set` tool;
- a value pydantic can't serialize to JSON, e.g. an instance of an arbitrary class inside the dict or set.

Bare `list` / `tuple` tools are unchanged unless they pass `structured_output=True`, which used to raise. Only a bare `list` / `tuple` as the whole annotation is opted out; nested ones (`list | None`, `dict | list`, `list[list]`) keep the wrapped schema they publish today.

## Types of changes

## Checklist

## Additional context

This differs from the branch proposed in #3725, which also wraps bare `list` / `tuple`; the reason is the double-send above. Unparameterized `typing.List` / `typing.Tuple` are unchanged (still wrapped like `list[Any]`).

prompt:

# Retry a tool call once after a HeaderMismatch rejection

Fixes #3483.

## What was wrong

On a 2026-07-28 Streamable HTTP connection, `Client.call_tool` for a tool with `x-mcp-header` arguments failed with `-32020` (`HeaderMismatch`) unless that client had already listed the tool. It also kept failing when the tool's schema gained an annotation after it was listed.

The spec's [Client Behavior](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic/transports/streamable-http#client-behavior) section says a client SHOULD answer that rejection by calling `tools/list` and retrying the request. The client raised instead. The TypeScript SDK already retries.

## What changes

`Client.call_tool` now performs that recovery. The signature is unchanged and there are no new public names.

- On an `MCPError` with code `-32020`, on a 2026-07-28 connection:
    - the tool listing is refetched from the server, following cursors until a page lists the tool
    - the same call is resent once, with the `Mcp-Param-*` headers the current schema asks for
- A second rejection is raised. There is no second retry.
- One timeout bounds the whole re-list, not each page: the `read_timeout_seconds` passed to `call_tool`, or the client's own `read_timeout_seconds` when none is passed.
- If the re-list fails, the original `-32020` is raised with that failure as its cause, and the call is not resent. That covers:
    - an error response, or any other `MCPError`
    - a `tools/list` page that fails validation (`pydantic.ValidationError`)
    - the timeout elapsing (`TimeoutError`)

## What users will notice

- A call that used to raise `-32020` because the tool was not listed, or because its schema had changed, now succeeds.
    - On the wire: `tools/call` (rejected), `tools/list`, `tools/call`.
- A `-32020` that a re-list cannot cure is still raised, after those extra requests.
- The cost of a recovery is one `tools/list` request per page, up to the page that lists the tool, plus one resend.
    - For a single-page catalog that is the whole listing, once per recovered call.
    - A client that lists tools before calling them never pays it.
- The cursor walk stops after 100 pages, the same cap the server uses when it resolves a tool's schema for this validation. A listing whose cursors never end cannot hang a call: after 100 pages the call is resent once anyway.
- The read timeout in effect (per call, or the client's default) applies separately to the rejected call, to the re-list as a whole, and to the resend, so a recovered call can take up to three times that value.
    - With neither set there is no time bound on the re-list, as for any other request; the 100-page cap still applies.
- An `except MCPError` around `call_tool` sees the `-32020` in each of those re-list failures; the reason is on `__cause__`.
- Cancelling the caller during a recovery still cancels it.
- The re-list replaces the client's cached tool listing, so a later `list_tools()` served from the cache returns the current schema.
- `-32020` is a rejection before dispatch, so the resend does not run a tool twice on a conforming server. A tool handler that raises `-32020` itself is run twice on a 2026-07-28 connection.
- Unchanged:
    - connections on earlier protocol versions, where a `-32020` is raised as it arrives
    - `ClientSession.call_tool`, which still sends once and leaves the recovery to its caller
    - every call that does not fail with `-32020`

## Docs

- The Header parameters page gains one line saying that a call for a tool the client has not listed is rejected, and that `Client` then lists the tools and resends it once.
- The migration guide's section on `Mcp-Param-*` header validation is removed, along with the link to it from the What's new page. The feature is new in 2026-07-28, so it is not a v1-to-v2 migration topic.
- The translated pages are not regenerated here; their What's new pages still carry the old link until the next translation run.

## Not included

- A public way to pre-load the header map, the other h

title: Record JSON-RPC error responses on the client OpenTelemetry span
prompt:
Make the change described below to the repository in the current directory.
Work until the change is complete. Do not open a pull request, push, or fetch anything from the network.

# Record JSON-RPC error responses on the client OpenTelemetry span

Fixes #3174.

When the peer answers a request with a JSON-RPC error, the client span (`MCP send <method>`) ends looking exactly like a success: status unset, no error attributes. The caller still gets its `MCPError`; only the trace is wrong. This records the error on the span.

## What was wrong

- `send_raw_request` receives the response inside the span, but an error response was only turned into `MCPError` after the span had closed, so the span never saw a failure.
- A timeout or a failed write on the same span was already `ERROR`, so the most common failure was the one missing from traces.
- The OpenTelemetry MCP semantic convention (Development status) says of the client span: ["All JSON-RPC error codes SHOULD be considered errors."](https://github.com/open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai/blob/b31e9e8ea26ac1c086d3313d474e31d7c3f391ae/docs/gen-ai/mcp.md#L201-L204)

## What changes

- In `JSONRPCDispatcher.send_raw_request`, an error response now sets the status and two attributes on the span while it is still open. The `MCPError` is raised where it was before.
- The "connection closed" outcome handed to waiting requests is now one shared module-level value, so the span can tell it apart from an error the peer sent, including one that uses the same code.
- No public API changes, and nothing changes on the wire.

## What users will notice

- A client span whose request was answered with a JSON-RPC error now has what the convention asks for:
    - status `ERROR`, with the peer's error message as the [description](https://github.com/open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai/blob/b31e9e8ea26ac1c086d3313d474e31d7c3f391ae/docs/gen-ai/mcp.md#L128-L132)
    - [`error.type`](https://github.com/open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai/blob/b31e9e8ea26ac1c086d3313d474e31d7c3f391ae/docs/gen-ai/mcp.md#L180-L185) set to the error code as a string (for example `"-32602"`)
    - [`rpc.response.status_code`](https://github.com/open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai/blob/b31e9e8ea26ac1c086d3313d474e31d7c3f391ae/docs/gen-ai/mcp.md#L166) set to the same string, since the response contains an error code
- The same applies to requests a server sends to a client, such as sampling and elicitation.
- No exception event is added to the span, and the `MCPError` the caller receives is unchanged.

## The `server/discover` probe

- With the default `mode="auto"`, each connect to a server that does not know `server/discover` now produces one `ERROR` client span for that probe, even though the connect succeeds.
- The request did fail, and the convention has no exception for it.
- A probe that times out was already `ERROR` before this change, so probe failures are now consistent.
- To filter these spans, match on the attribute `mcp.method.name = server/discover`. The error code is not a reliable key, because it varies by server and transport (`-32601`, `-32602`, `-32600` and `-32603` have all been seen).
- For a server known to be on an older protocol version, `mode="legacy"` sends no probe.

## What is not included

- A request abandoned because the connection closed while it was waiting keeps the span it has today (status unset). No response arrived, so there is no response code to record.
- Spans for timeouts, failed writes, cancelled calls and successful requests are as before.

## How it was checked

- The test fails on `main` (the failed span is `UNSET`) and passes with the change.
- `./scripts/test` passes with 100% coverage; ruff and pyright are clean.

# Omit an empty _meta and empty params from outbound requests

Fixes #3473.

On a connection that uses the `initialize` handshake (2025-11-25 and earlier), v2 put `"_meta": {}` in the params of every request it sent, `initialize` included. An empty `_meta` is valid per the spec, but v1 never sent one and some servers reject it, which made them unreachable from a v2 client.

## What was wrong

- `JSONRPCDispatcher.send_raw_request` attached the `_meta` dict before trace context was injected into it, so it went out even when nothing was ever put in it.
- That is the default case: no OpenTelemetry SDK configured, no progress callback, no caller-supplied meta.
- Requests with no params of their own, such as `ping` and `tools/list`, went out as `"params": {"_meta": {}}`.

## What changes on the wire

`_meta` is now sent only when it has content, and a request left with no params is sent without a `params` member.

Before:

After:

- This is the shape v1 sent.
- `params` is optional in the schema for every request that can end up with none (`ping`, the list requests, `roots/list`), and JSON-RPC 2.0 allows omitting it.

## What users will notice

- Requests from a client on a 2025-11-25 or earlier connection:
    - no `_meta` unless there is a progress token, caller-supplied meta, or trace context to carry
    - no `params` member on `ping` and on list requests without a cursor
- Server-initiated requests (`ping`, `roots/list`, sampling, elicitation) change the same way.
- When both ends run this SDK and the sender supplied no meta, the receiving side sees what it already sees from any other client:
    - a server handler gets `ctx.meta` as `None` rather than `{}`
    - server middleware gets `ctx.params` as `None` for a request with no params
    - sampling and elicitation callbacks get `params.meta` as `None` rather than `{}`
- An empty `_meta` passed by the caller (for example `send_ping(meta={})`) is not sent, and neither is an empty params object.

- Tracing. With an OpenTelemetry tracer provider configured, `traceparent` is still injected into `_meta` on every outbound request, including ones with no other params.

# Let MCPServer opt out of serving subscriptions/listen

Fixes #3357.

## What was wrong

`MCPServer` always registers a `subscriptions/listen` handler, and there was no supported way to leave it out.

- On a 2026-07-28 connection every `MCPServer` advertises `listChanged` for tools, prompts and resources, and `resources.subscribe`, as true, including a server whose catalog never changes.
- A client that acts on those flags, as the TypeScript client does, opens a listen stream, and the stream stays open until the client closes it.
- On hosts that bill per request duration, each of those streams runs to the platform timeout. #3493 has measurements from one such deployment.
- The only ways to avoid it were removing the handler through a private attribute or rewriting the server on the low-level `Server`.

## What changes

The existing `subscriptions` constructor parameter accepts one more value, `False`. Nothing else is added: no new parameter, name or export.

- The type goes from `SubscriptionBus | None` to `SubscriptionBus | Literal[False] | None`.
- `False` means the server does not serve `subscriptions/listen`.
- `None` (the default) and a bus mean what they did before.

## What users will notice

Existing servers: nothing. The default is unchanged, so a server that does not pass `subscriptions=False` advertises and serves listen exactly as before.

A server built with `subscriptions=False`:

- `server/discover` at 2026-07-28 reports `tools.listChanged`, `prompts.listChanged`, `resources.listChanged` and `resources.subscribe` as false.
- A `subscriptions/listen` request is answered immediately with `-32601` Method not found (HTTP 404 on Streamable HTTP), and no stream is opened.
- `ctx.notify_tools_changed()` and the other `ctx.notify_*` methods still succeed and reach nobody, so handler code is the same either way.
- Connections on earlier protocol versions behave as before.

## Not included

- Per-capability control, such as tool list changes on and resource subscriptions off. That belongs to the declared-capabilities work in #2896; this option is all or nothing.
- Any change to the default, to the low-level `Server`, or to how an open listen stream behaves.

## How it was checked

    - with `subscriptions=False`, discover reports the four flags false and `client.listen()` fails with `METHOD_NOT_FOUND`
    - with `subscriptions=False`, a tool that calls `ctx.notify_tools_changed()` still returns its result
    - a default server still reports the four flags true
- The two `subscriptions=False` tests fail on `main` and pass with this change.
- Over stateless Streamable HTTP with `json_response=True`: a default server acknowledges and holds the stream; with `subscriptions=False` discover shows the four flags false and listen returns 404 with `-32601`.
- `./scripts/test` passes with 100% coverage; ruff and pyright are clean.

## Docs

The option is documented on the Subscriptions page.

- A small diagram at the top of "Scaling past one process": two replicas behind a load balancer, each with its own in-memory bus. The listen stream is subscribed to one bus, a tool call publishes to the other, and nothing connects the two.
- The two ways out behind a load balancer: give every replica a shared `SubscriptionBus`, or turn change notifications off.

# Keep the live Context when a prompt or template annotates Context[T]

Fixes #3235.

## What was wrong

A prompt or resource-template function annotated `ctx: Context[AppState]` was handed an empty `Context` instead of the one for the request. The same annotation on a tool worked, and bare `Context` worked everywhere.

- Prompts and templates validate their call arguments with pydantic, and the injected context went through that validation too.
- `Context[AppState]` is a separate class at runtime, so pydantic rebuilt the request's plain `Context` as a new instance, without the private attributes that hold the request.
- Two symptoms:
    - `ctx.request_context`, `ctx.request_id` and `ctx.session` raised `Context is not available outside of a request`, which the client saw as an internal error.
    - `ctx.protocol_version`, `ctx.input_responses` and `ctx.request_state` read as `None`. A multi-round-trip prompt or template never saw the answers and kept asking until the client raised `InputRequiredRoundsExceededError`.

## What changes

- `Context` gets a wrap-mode model validator that returns an existing `Context` instance unchanged and leaves any other input to normal validation.
- Prompts and templates are otherwise untouched: client arguments are cast and rejected exactly as before.
- No names, parameters or defaults change, and nothing changes on the wire.
- Docs: the "tool-only" warning on the Lifespan page and the matching paragraph in the migration guide are removed.

## What users will notice

# Describe the ID-JAG confidential-client rule as SDK policy, not a SEP-990 requirement

Fixes #3598.

The SDK only lets confidential clients (ones with a shared secret) use the ID-JAG `jwt-bearer` grant, on both the client provider and the built-in authorization server. The docs, several comments and one error message said SEP-990 requires that. It doesn't, and this corrects the text.

This does **not** change which clients the built-in authorization server accepts.

## What the documents say

- The [enterprise-managed authorization extension](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/ext-auth/blob/fb374c7db2b34f18ca9183882e0beecdf661892b/specification/stable/enterprise-managed-authorization.mdx#L210-L233) (SEP-990)
    - Section 5: the client authenticates with its credentials as registered. A client that isn't pre-registered "can use its Client ID Metadata Document as its client ID, and optionally authenticate using private_key_jwt".
    - Section 5.1 defers to the IETF draft's processing rules and adds an audience rule. It says nothing about confidential clients.
- [draft-ietf-oauth-identity-assertion-authz-grant-04, section 9.1](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-oauth-identity-assertion-authz-grant-04.html#section-9.1): "This specification SHOULD only be supported for confidential clients."
- [RFC 7521, section 1](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7521#section-1): whether client authentication is needed with an assertion grant is a policy decision "at the discretion of the authorization server".

So the restriction is the SDK's policy, adopting the draft's SHOULD.

## What changed

- `docs/client/identity-assertion.md`
    - "A confidential client" now says the IETF profile recommends the grant for confidential clients only, RFC 7521 leaves the policy to the authorization server, and the SDK takes the conservative reading on both sides.
    - "The authorization server" gains one bullet:
        - refusing public clients is SDK policy
        - the built-in server authenticates clients by shared secret only: it has no `private_key_jwt` support and doesn't resolve Client ID Metadata Documents yet (#1801), so a client identified by one can't use this grant against it
        - a deployment that wants a different policy can swap the `/token` route that `create_auth_routes` returns for its own

- `IdentityAssertionOAuthProvider`
    - The `client_secret` docstring no longer cites SEP-990 section 5.1.
    - The `ValueError` for an empty `client_secret` now reads `client_secret is required: this provider supports confidential clients only` (it said "SEP-990 mandates a confidential client").
- The two `examples/snippets` identity-assertion files had the same attribution, one line each.

## What users will notice

Only the new `ValueError` text. The exception type and the condition that raises it are the same, and the token endpoint still answers a client with no secret with `unauthorized_client`.

Support for Client ID Metadata Document clients in the built-in authorization server, with or without `private_key_jwt`. That is #1801. Translated pages aren't regenerated here.

# Add AuthSettings.validate_token_resource to check a bearer token's resource

Adds an opt-in `AuthSettings.validate_token_resource`. When set, the bearer gate only accepts a token that the `TokenVerifier` reports as issued for `resource_server_url` (via `AccessToken.resource`); a token reporting another resource, or none, gets the same 401 as an unrecognized token. Leaving it unset on a resource server emits an `MCPDeprecationWarning` and behaves as off; 3.0 makes it the default there.

## Motivation and Context

The resource-server gate checks scopes and expiry but has never compared the token's RFC 8707 resource indicator with the server's own identifier; the interaction suite records this as the `hosting:auth:aud-validation` divergence. In practice that comparison was left to each `TokenVerifier`, without the docs or the protocol docstring saying so.

This does two things:

- Documents the contract. `TokenVerifier.verify_token` and `docs/run/authorization.md` now say to put the token's audience in `AccessToken.resource`, and that otherwise confirming the token was issued for this server is the verifier's job.
- Adds the option for deployments whose authorization server binds tokens to the `resource` the client requested (which is what MCP clients send). It isn't enforced by default because `AccessToken.resource` gets populated in lots of ways today (IdP-specific audience identifiers, for instance), and doing so unconditionally would reject valid tokens in those setups; instead an unset value warns so each deployment chooses `True` or `False` once. `RefreshToken` gains an optional `resource` so providers can carry the binding through the refresh grant.

The comparison is URL equality with a trailing slash tolerated; both sides go through `AnyHttpUrl` so host case and an explicit default port don't matter. It lives in `BearerAuthBackend` (new keyword-only `resource_server_url`) so a refused token never reaches `get_access_token()` or custom routes, and a refusal logs both values at warning level.

## Breaking Changes

None. Unset behaves as off (with the deprecation warning); `BearerAuthBackend(verifier)` and existing verifiers behave as before. Setting it to `True` without a `resource_server_url` raises at construction.

When a tool's return type is self-referential, pydantic emits the output schema as `{"$defs": {...}, "$ref": "#/$defs/Node"}` with no `type` at the root. `Tool.outputSchema` requires `type: "object"` at the root on 2025-11-25 and earlier, so one such tool failed the *entire* `tools/list` result for every legacy-negotiated client (`Handler returned an invalid result`). # Hand TypedDict tool results to pydantic natively

MCPServer now validates and serializes `TypedDict` tool results through pydantic's own TypedDict support instead of mirroring the TypedDict into a hand-built `BaseModel`.

Fixes #3224
Fixes #3227

## Motivation and Context

The hand-built mirror in `_create_model_from_typeddict` was the common root of a few problems with `TypedDict` return types:

- Optional keys (`NotRequired`, `total=False`) got a `None` default and were dumped as `null`, so a tool that left one out produced `structuredContent` that violated its own `outputSchema` (`{"type": "integer", "default": null}`) and the client rejected the call (#3224). This affected every Python version.
- The field types came from `typing.get_type_hints`, which leaves `NotRequired`/`Required` in place on 3.10 and `ReadOnly` in place on 3.10–3.12; `create_model` rejects bare qualifiers, so registration raised `PydanticForbiddenQualifier` (#3227, plus the unreported `ReadOnly` variant).
- The TypedDict's docstring and any `Annotated[..., Field(...)]` metadata never reached the schema, and constraints weren't enforced.

Nested and wrapped TypedDicts (`-> list[Person]`, a TypedDict inside a model) already went through pydantic natively and had none of these issues, so this makes the top-level case consistent with them.

What changes:

- `TypedDict` returns are handled by a `TypeAdapter` over the TypedDict itself; `_create_model_from_typeddict` is gone.
- pydantic refuses `typing.TypedDict` below Python 3.12, so on 3.10/3.11 a stdlib TypedDict return type is rebuilt as an equivalent `typing_extensions.TypedDict` when the validator is built (per-key required/optional derived the way pydantic does it; docstring, `__module__`/`__qualname__`, `__pydantic_config__` and `ReadOnly` carried over). `output_model` stays the class the user declared. Only the top-level class is rebuilt: a stdlib TypedDict nested inside one (or config inherited from a stdlib base) still needs `typing_extensions` below 3.12 and otherwise falls back to unstructured output with an INFO log; wrapped forms (`list[StdTD]`, `StdTD | None`, ...) raise pydantic's "use typing_extensions.TypedDict" at registration exactly as they do on `main`. Delete when 3.11 support is dropped.
- `FuncMetadata` derives a private validator (and `output_schema`, unless one is given) from `output_model` when it is constructed; `func_metadata()` constructs it inside the existing "not serializable for structured output" fallback, so unsupported return types still degrade (or raise `InvalidSignature` with `structured_output=True`). The fields are read live: code that clears or assigns `output_schema`/`output_model` on a registered tool's `fn_metadata` keeps working, and the validator is rebuilt if `output_model` is reassigned. `FuncMetadata.output_model` is the TypedDict class for TypedDict tools (still the model class for everything else); its annotation widens to `type[Any] | None`.
- Results are validated with `by_name=True` as well as by alias, so a return type declaring `Field(alias=...)` accepts the Python-side keys a tool naturally returns while `structuredContent` carries the aliases the schema advertises.

This supersedes #3225 — thanks @sainikhiljuluri for the thorough reports and the initial fix, and @gingeekrishna for the `typing_extensions.get_type_hints` pointer. I went with the native route rather than `exclude_unset` because `exclude_unset` recurses into nested models (a `BaseModel` with defaults inside a TypedDict would lose its defaulted fields) and the mirror would still publish `default: null` and drop metadata.

## Breaking Changes

No code changes needed. Observable differences, mostly for TypedDict tools:

# Let Client take StdioServerParameters directly

`Client` resolves its transport from the type of its one positional argument: a server object connects in-process, a `str` is a Streamable HTTP URL, and anything else is entered as a `Transport`. stdio was the odd one out — you had to write `Client(stdio_client(StdioServerParameters(...)))`, and the transports page had a paragraph explaining why the parameters object alone doesn't work. This adds the missing arm:

`Client(stdio_client(server, errlog=...))` still works and is now documented as the way to redirect the child's stderr (the one knob `stdio_client` has beyond the params).

## Motivation and Context

Connecting to a local server over stdio is one of the two normal ways to use a client, and it was the only one that needed a wrapper and a second import. The examples harness already carried a `# becomes Client(params) once that overload lands` note for exactly this.

Deliberately not in scope: accepting `SseServerParameters` / `StreamableHttpParameters` (the URL string already covers HTTP; SSE is legacy), and any string/path inference.

## Breaking Changes

None. Additive: `Client(stdio_client(...))` keeps working unchanged. Passing a bare `StdioServerParameters` previously failed at `async with` (it isn't an async context manager), so no working code changes meaning.
